alternates: The Economy Is Growing. Why Are Paychecks Falling Behind?
Growth, Jobs and Real Wages in 2026
stories.question: Is the US economy booming, and are workers' paychecks keeping up?
stories.whyWatch: One side says the economy is booming, the other says families are worse off, and both point at real numbers. GDP, the jobs report and real earnings show which parts of each claim hold.
stories.tension: GDP is growing and unemployment is low, yet real hourly pay fell over the past year. A booming economy and shrinking paychecks sound incompatible, but they are measuring different things.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Official GDP growth, unemployment and payroll figures for 2026, and real average hourly earnings over the past year and at the start of 2026.

stories.premise: Real GDP grew at 2.5% and 2.2% annual rates in the first two quarters of 2026, about trend growth: solid expansion rather than a boom. Unemployment was 4.2% in September and has stayed between 4.1% and 4.3% since March, a low rate, but payroll growth was weak (+29,000 in September) and the jobs report does not define full employment, so 'full employment' is a judgement, not a measurement. Real average hourly earnings rose 1.2% in the year to January 2026, then turned negative from April and were down 0.7% in the year to September as prices rose 3.7% and pay 3.0%. These are averages for all employees, not the median worker. So growth and falling real pay coexisted in 2026, but on the employment side it was steady rather than strong.

arc.hook: The economy grew every quarter this year, and the average worker's pay bought less in September than a year earlier.
arc.conflict: Supporters call it a boom; critics say households are going backwards. Each cites a real statistic.
arc.evidence: GDP growth against trend, the unemployment rate and payroll growth, then real hourly earnings in January and September 2026.
arc.resolution: The economy is growing at about its usual pace, not booming. Unemployment is low but hiring is slow. Real pay rose into early 2026 and has fallen since prices jumped in the spring.
arc.takeaway: When someone says the economy is booming, ask which number: output, jobs or what a paycheck buys. In 2026 they point in different directions.

coherence.explanation: One question, is the economy booming and are households sharing in it, answered by growth, the job market and real wages; the January 2026 real-wage reading shows the turn.

stories.question: Is gas cheaper now than it was under Biden?
stories.whyWatch: The claim was true for a while and then stopped being true, and people still repeat it both ways. The EIA's monthly price record shows exactly when it flipped and what drove it.
stories.tension: Gas was cheaper through 2025 and into early 2026 than the Biden-era average. Then it jumped in March 2026. Which statement is 'now' depends on the month.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Monthly US regular gasoline prices for 2021-2026, the average and peak over the previous administration, weekly prices around March 2026, and crude oil prices over the same period.

stories.premise: Over February 2021 to January 2025 regular gasoline averaged $3.46 a gallon, peaking at $4.93 in June 2022. Through 2025 it averaged $3.10, below that average every month, though about level with the last months of the previous administration; it was $2.89 in December 2025 and $2.81 and $2.91 in January and February 2026. Then it jumped: from $3.02 in the first week of March 2026 to $4.50 by mid-May, and the monthly average was $4.48 in May and $4.36 in September, well above the Biden-era average though below the 2022 peak. Crude oil moved with it: WTI averaged $97 in September 2026 against a Biden-era average of about $80. Pump prices tracked crude under both administrations, which supports the view that gas follows the world oil market, and the March jump coincides with the Iran conflict; both rest on timing and co-movement in price series, which cannot rule out other causes. All prices are nominal.

arc.hook: Gas is cheaper than under Biden: true in January 2026, false by April.
arc.conflict: Supporters quote the 2025 prices; critics quote the spring and autumn of 2026. Both are reading the same EIA table.
arc.evidence: The monthly price line from 2021 to 2026 against the Biden-era average and peak, the weekly jump in March 2026, then crude oil on the same chart.
arc.resolution: Gas was cheaper than the Biden-era average through February 2026 and has been dearer since March, though still below the 2022 peak. Pump prices moved with crude both times.
arc.takeaway: A gas price claim is only as good as its date. Check the month, and check what crude did.

stories.title: How High Is Inflation, Really?
alternates: Is There Really No Inflation? The September 2026 Numbers
Inflation in 2026: High, Low, or Neither?
stories.question: How high is US inflation right now, compared with the target, the past and the 2022 peak?
stories.whyWatch: People are told there is no inflation, that it is low by historical standards, and that it is far below the peak. The official CPI shows which of these comparisons hold and which pick a convenient baseline.
stories.tension: Inflation is less than half its 2022 peak, which lets one side call it low. It is also higher than when the administration took office and has been above target for five years, which lets the other side call it high.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The latest monthly and twelve-month CPI readings, the recent three-month pace, the CPI history back to before the pandemic, and the 2022 peak.
evidenceAvailable: BLS CPI release, September 2026: wrong (0.95, direct)
BLS CPI, earnings and jobs series 2019-2026: wrong (0.85, direct)
BLS CPI, earnings and jobs series 2019-2026: right (0.7, direct)

stories.premise: Consumer prices rose 0.6% in September 2026 and 3.7% over twelve months, so the claim that there is no inflation is wrong. 3.7% is below the 9.1% peak of June 2022 but above every reading in 2024 and 2025, above the roughly 1.5-2.5% pace before the pandemic, and above the 3.0% of January 2025. It was a different story in January 2026: 2.4%, tied for the lowest reading since early 2021 and about the pre-pandemic pace, so 'low by historical standards' was fair then (in a series that starts in 2019) and stopped being fair by September. Prices rose about 1.1% from June to September, a 4.6% annualized pace, so the recent three months were not below target. The twelve-month CPI rate has been at least 2.3% every month since March 2021; the Fed's 2% target is defined on a different index (PCE), which usually runs somewhat lower, so 'above target' is shown on CPI. And a falling inflation rate does not mean falling prices: from January 2023 to September 2024 the rate fell from 6.4% to 2.4% while the price level kept rising.

arc.hook: Depending on who you listen to, there is no inflation, or it is the worst in years. Both cannot be right.
arc.conflict: Each side picks a baseline: the 2022 peak makes today look low; January 2025 and the Fed target make it look high.
arc.evidence: The September 2026 CPI, then the same number against history, the peak, January 2025, the recent three months and the target, then the rate against the price level.
arc.resolution: Inflation is 3.7%: far below the 2022 peak, but above target, above the start of 2025 and above any year from 2024 to 2025, and not zero by any measure.
arc.takeaway: When you hear an inflation comparison, ask what it is being compared with, and remember that a lower rate still means higher prices.

coherence.explanation: One question, how high inflation is right now, answered against zero, the Fed target, history (in January 2026 and now), the 2022 peak and January 2025, plus the common confusion between a falling rate and falling prices.

stories.title: Who Really Pays for Tariffs?
alternates: Do Tariffs Raise Prices? What the 2025 Data Show
Tariffs: Do Foreign Exporters Pay, or Do We?
stories.question: Who actually pays for tariffs, and do they raise the prices Americans pay?
stories.whyWatch: Politicians say foreign countries pay the tariffs; critics say consumers do. New York Fed research on the 2025 tariffs measured where the cost actually landed and how much reached store shelves.
stories.tension: If foreign exporters cut their prices to keep selling, Americans pay nothing extra. If they do not, the cost lands on US importers and then on shoppers, including for goods made at home.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Import-price data on how much of the 2025 tariffs foreign exporters absorbed, estimates of pass-through to consumer prices for imported and domestic goods, and how the effect evolves over time.

stories.premise: Foreign exporters absorbed little of the 2025 tariffs: US importers bore about 94% of the incidence from January to August 2025 and 86% by November, according to New York Fed import-price regressions. Of a tariff increase, about 26% reached consumer goods prices within a year, and not at once: about half of the direct effect is in shop prices after three months and all of it by six, while surveyed firms describe fixed-price contracts and deliberately gradual increases, so retailers do not reprice the moment a tariff is announced. About a third of the consumer price effect came through domestically made goods, as US producers paid more for imported inputs and faced less competition. These are estimates relative to less-exposed goods, covering goods only, and they leave out the exchange rate and monetary policy. Over time the tariff effect raised the goods price level by close to 3% at its February 2026 peak and stays positive, while its contribution to twelve-month inflation is forecast to fade, so tariffs look like a rise in the level of prices more than lasting inflation; but business surveys find firms spreading increases over long periods, so in practice the one-time rise is drawn out, especially when tariffs keep changing.

arc.hook: A tariff is a tax paid at the US border. The fight is over who ends up carrying it.
arc.conflict: One side says foreign exporters cut their prices and eat the cost; the other says Americans pay it all at the checkout.
arc.evidence: The New York Fed's incidence estimates, then the pass-through to consumer prices for imported and domestic goods, then the price level against the inflation rate over time.
arc.resolution: US importers paid most of the 2025 tariffs, and part of that cost reached consumer prices, including for goods made at home. The effect raises the price level and fades from the inflation rate, but slowly.
arc.takeaway: A tariff that foreign sellers do not absorb is paid at home, by firms first and shoppers over the following year.

coherence.explanation: One question, who pays for tariffs and do they raise prices, answered by incidence, pass-through to consumer and domestic prices, how fast it arrives, and whether the effect is one-off. Whether tariffs make the country wealthier is a different question with no study.

stories.title: Do Gas Prices Really Rise Every Summer?
alternates: The Summer Gas Price Myth: When Prices Actually Peak
Why Gas Peaks in May, Not August
stories.question: Do gas prices really go up every summer?
stories.whyWatch: Every spring someone blames the summer driving season for higher gas prices. Sixteen years of EIA monthly prices show when the seasonal rise happens and when it stops.
stories.tension: Prices do climb from winter. But if summer driving were the cause, the peak should come in July or August, and it usually does not.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Monthly US regular gasoline prices over many years, comparing January, May and August.
evidenceAvailable: EIA regular gasoline, monthly: partly (0.65, direct)
stories.premise: In the EIA's monthly record for 2010-2025, the May price was above the January price in 15 of 16 years, so there is a seasonal rise from winter into spring. But May was at or above August in 13 of those 16 years (2024: $3.60 in May against $3.39 in August), so the seasonal peak usually comes in late spring and prices plateau or drift down through the driving season itself. The claim is right that prices rise seasonally and wrong about when they top out. The price series shows the pattern, not its cause.

arc.hook: Gas goes up every summer. Except the record says it usually peaks before summer starts.
arc.conflict: The common explanation is summer road trips; the timing of the peak does not fit it well.
arc.evidence: Sixteen years of January, May and August prices side by side.
arc.resolution: Prices rise from winter into spring in nearly every year, and usually level off or ease from May to August.
arc.takeaway: If you are waiting for summer to pass before gas gets cheaper, the seasonal high has usually already come by May.

coherence.explanation: One claim, one question: do pump prices rise every year into the summer driving season.
